content.title: Surge of tax refund scams detected ahead of IRS deadline: What to watch for
content.text: Related video above: Reports of scam texts are on the rise (NEXSTAR) – Experts are warning of a surge in scam websites created to take advantage of taxpayers trying to file their returns online before the deadline. A new report from cybersecurity company Check Point Software found a notable increase in tax-related domains that started in September 2025, with 1 in every 15 classified as malicious or suspicious. In March, the volume of website creation jumped up, as did the level of risk, with Check Point finding 1 in every 10 new tax-related domains to be a potential threat. “Especially now, with AI, it’s going to be easier to clone a tax provider, a government website, [or] create something that has the same look and feel, but some slight back end differences,” Check Point Senior Architect Greg Pepper told Nexstar. “Before you needed to know a little bit about the technology to maybe run some of these things, whereas now there might be tools to help you … create more sophisticated lookalikes than ever before.” What do the phishing attacks look like? A taxpayer who clicks on a link to one of the portals might believe it to be a legitimate government site, as some of the fake IRS portals look exactly like the real website. (Credit: Check Point Software) “The websites lure victims with fake ‘tax refund’ offers, promising unusually high payouts such as weekly payments of $1,400 or a one‑time payment of $38,700,” according to the report. “Victims are then prompted to submit sensitive personal information — including full name, Social Security number, phone number, and email address — followed by an identity verification process, strongly suggesting large‑scale data harvesting.” Check Point analysts suspect that phishing attempts like the site above are part of a coordinated effort, as the company found a number of similar, suspicious urls that include, for example, 2025irswebsiteislive[.]live and irstax-refund[.]xyz. The phishing attacks extend beyond the U.S., the report found, with at least one malicious email campaign using a spoofed email address from Spain’s tax authority to circulate malware. Meantime, the IRS is also warning of scammers who have created their own versions of the IRS’ online tax calculator, which allows taxpayers to determine their refunds. “Be wary of calculators or websites that guarantee a big payday or an unusually large, unexpected refund,” the IRS said. How to keep your information safe The IRS also warns that tax-season impersonation scams can take multiple forms, using disaster relief, refunds, lottery winnings, government programs and more as entry points to gain access to a victim’s personal information. The IRS and Check Point recommend taxpayers do the following to stay safe: Always verify any URL in a tax-related email or text message before clicking Don’t trust unsolicited messages that promise large refunds or threaten penalties Don’t send sensitive personal information like one’s Social Security number through an emailed link Enable multi-factor authentication wherever you file your taxes or manage your money Go directly to the IRS website, www.irs.gov, instead of clicking through via third-party link. Forward any suspicious-looking emails to phishing@irs.gov and then delete the email. Pepper said scammers will look to capitalize on any highly-anticipated date when people are looking to spend or receive money. “The common sense that we’re using around tax day preparation and being alert for scammers, we should be prepared and planning for Black Friday, or the next Amazon Prime Day,” Pepper said. The IRS tax filing deadline for 2026 is April 15. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed.
